name: Diego Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Diego, and thanks for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, no worries. I run a front-end loader on the ROM pad at a zinc and lead mine, the run-of-mine pad, which is the big yard where the trucks dump ore before it goes into the crusher. My job is to keep the crusher fed, blending the ore from different piles so the plant gets the right mix. Twelve-hour shifts, mostly days. I've been on the loader about a year, before that I was a labourer on the same site.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's a proper job with a ladder. You start on the shovel, you get your loader ticket, and if you keep your nose clean you move up. The hard part right now is money, because Megan and I are getting married in April and weddings cost a fortune, and I'm still on the junior loader rate. I coach the under-twelves football on Saturdays, and some weeks that's the only thing that doesn't cost me anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read five pictures of the future. The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now everyone can stop talking about it. At the pub I'd probably say that the people selling it were the only ones who got rich. I'm not big online, I mostly just look at the football club page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truth is I'd be relieved. I've got a wedding in April and a ladder to climb here. If nothing changes, I keep climbing and maybe in five years I'm on the big loaders or a leading hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing. Work, wedding, coach the kids. Megan and I would keep putting a bit aside for a deposit on a house after the wedding. I'd ask about the next ticket, the bigger loader, maybe next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How are you paying for the wedding on a junior rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. Megan's parents are helping with the hall, her dad insisted, and my mum's making the cake. We cut the guest list from a hundred and forty to ninety, which was its own war. Every bit of spare money till April goes there, so the house deposit is more of an idea right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, now and then. Megan made me use one to help with my speech, and it was okay, but I rewrote most of it because it sounded like a greeting card. At work, no, it's a loader, it doesn't need a chatbot.

S0.say: I'd say everyone can stop talking about it now and that the people selling AI were the only ones who got rich. I'd say that at the pub rather than online.
S0.think: I think I'd be relieved, with a wedding in April and a ladder to climb at the mine. If nothing changes, I keep climbing and maybe become a leading hand in five years.
S0.do: Keeps working, gets married in April and keeps coaching. Saves a little with his fiancée towards a house deposit after the wedding and asks about the bigger loader ticket next year.
S0.quote: It was okay, but I rewrote most of it because it sounded like a greeting card.
S0.fieldNote: He sees the mine as a ladder and the quiet picture lets him keep climbing. The wedding is the dominant money story, with both families helping. He's used AI once or twice, reluctantly, and kept his own words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business, companies have to stay competitive, and if machines are cheaper they'll use them. But I'd say they should keep the apprenticeships going so young guys have somewhere to start, like I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the ROM pad is a pretty obvious one to automate. It's piles and a crusher and a set mix. If the loader could read the ore grades off a screen and blend by itself, they'd do it. I'd be a bit worried, not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see what the company actually does first, how many jobs, what training. If guys getting the remote or maintenance training kept their jobs, I'd go for it in the second round. Meanwhile I'd keep the wedding on track but maybe cut the honeymoon to something closer to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it'd be in the back of my head every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned cutting the honeymoon. How would Megan feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be the one to suggest it, honestly. She's a teacher's aide and she's sensible. We were looking at an island trip and we'd probably drive up the coast instead. Fine by me, I get seasick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'young guys'. What about young women starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. There are two women on our crew and they're better on the loader than me, if I'm honest. I meant young people. Same thing applies, the apprenticeships are how anyone gets in.

S1.say: I'd say it's business and companies will use machines if they're cheaper. But they should keep apprenticeships going so young people have somewhere to start, like I did.
S1.think: I think the run-of-mine pad is an obvious one to automate, because it's piles, a crusher and a set mix. I'd be a bit worried, not panicking.
S1.do: Watches what the company actually does on jobs and training, then goes for remote or maintenance training in the second round if it's keeping people employed. Keeps the wedding on track but swaps the island honeymoon for a drive up the coast.
S1.feel: Uneasy, in the back of his mind every shift.
S1.quote: If the loader could read the ore grades off a screen and blend by itself, they'd do it.
S1.fieldNote: He accepts the company's right to automate but wants apprenticeships protected, fitting his traditional outlook. He waits for proof before training. When I pointed out his wording about 'young guys', he corrected himself readily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have to stand on their own feet and look after their families, but I'd also say this is too fast for anyone to plan for. Maybe the government needs to slow it down, which isn't something I'd normally say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I get married in April and maybe lose the job before our first anniversary. No savings, no house, no trade. That's not the start I promised Megan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, nothing changes that. But I'd cut the wedding right back, maybe just the church and a barbecue at her parents'. I'd put every bit of money aside, and I'd talk to my uncle about getting on his building crew, though robots would get there too, I suppose. Megan's job with kids might last longer, so we'd lean on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the floor's gone a bit soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut the wedding back. What would you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The church, because that's the point of it for us. And Mum's cake. Everything else can go, the band, the photographer, the hire suits. We'd get a cousin to take photos on her phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd normally not want the government to step in. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed. If a business beats you fairly, fine, that's competition. But if the whole world changes in two years, nobody had a fair go at getting ready. That's not a market, that's a flood.

S2.say: I'd say people have to look after their own families, but this is too fast for anyone to plan for. Maybe the government needs to slow it down, which isn't something I'd normally say.
S2.think: I think I could get married in April and lose my job before our first anniversary, with no savings, no house and no trade. That's not the start I promised Megan.
S2.do: Goes ahead with the wedding but cuts it to the church service and a barbecue, putting every bit of money aside. Asks his uncle about work on a building crew and leans on his wife's job as a teacher's aide lasting longer.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the floor has gone soft.
S2.quote: That's not a market, that's a flood.
S2.fieldNote: The speed of this picture pushes him past his usual free-market view to wanting government to slow things down. He'd protect the church ceremony and his mother's cake above everything. The sense of a broken promise to his fiancée drove his fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so get a trade, get your family sorted, don't wait for handouts. And I'd want the mine to run more apprenticeships, not fewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is tight but workable. I'd be thirty-two. I could get a trade ticket in that time if I started soon. The question is which trade lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the company in the first year and ask for a fitter apprenticeship, the mechanics who fix the machines. If they wouldn't, I'd look at the technical college. Megan and I would push the house deposit back and maybe wait a bit on kids, which would upset both our mums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a kind I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both mums would be upset about waiting on kids. Would they understand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eventually. My mum had me at twenty-two and thinks everyone's leaving it too late. I'd tell her it's not forever, just till I know there's a wage coming in. She'd say God provides, and I'd say God also likes a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a fitter rather than something away from mining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know the gear and the people, and the company might keep a few of us to look after the robots for a while. It's the next rung on the ladder I already know. I'm not a jump-off-a-cliff kind of guy.

S3.say: I'd say we have a few years, so get a trade, get your family sorted and don't wait for handouts. I'd want the mine to run more apprenticeships, not fewer.
S3.think: I think five years is tight but workable and I could get a trade ticket if I started soon. The question is which trade lasts.
S3.do: Asks the company for a fitter apprenticeship in the first year, or turns to the technical college if refused. Pushes back the house deposit and delays children with his wife, against both mothers' wishes.
S3.feel: Anxious, but in a way he can work with.
S3.quote: She'd say God provides, and I'd say God also likes a plan.
S3.fieldNote: He chooses the next rung on a ladder he knows rather than a leap elsewhere, which fits his steady nature. The cost lands on family timing, delaying children. His faith and practicality sit side by side easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Get a trade, save, look after your own. The government's job is to keep training places open, not to hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I'm pretty okay with. I'd be married, maybe a kid, maybe a trade. I'd want to have the trade before the kid, if I'm being smart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned, honeymoon included. Then in a year or two, once I've seen what the company does, I'd start the fitter apprenticeship. We'd still try for the house deposit, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like enough time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a trade before a kid. Have you and Megan talked about timing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of. She wants to start in two years. I'd want the apprenticeship underway by then. We'd work it out, we always do, usually her way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if the ten years were wasted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly people themselves, if they had the warning and did nothing. But also the schools and the companies that stopped training young people. When I started there were six apprentices on site. Now there's two.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty so there's no excuse: get a trade, save and look after your own. Government's job is to keep training places open, not hand out money.
S4.think: I think I'm pretty okay with ten years and could be married with a trade and maybe a child. I'd want the trade before the child, if I'm smart.
S4.do: Keeps the wedding and honeymoon as planned. Starts a fitter apprenticeship in a year or two once he's seen what the company does, and keeps saving more slowly for a house deposit.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, with enough time to do it right.
S4.quote: When I started there were six apprentices on site. Now there's two.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he gets his wedding back intact and plans a measured move into a trade. He holds individuals partly responsible, true to his views, but also blames the decline in apprenticeships. The six-to-two figure was a concrete grievance he clearly carries.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it lands right on top of the wedding and the first years of being married. What would help is apprenticeships, real ones, paid, with the company or the college, so a guy like me can move up a rung instead of falling off the ladder.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the kids I coach. They're eleven. By the time they finish school, what are they training for? Nobody can tell them, and their dads all work at the mine.

headlineQuote: By the time they finish school, what are they training for? Nobody can tell them, and their dads all work at the mine.
portrait: Diego Walsh is a 27-year-old junior front-end loader operator feeding the crusher at a zinc and lead mine, engaged to Megan, a teacher's aide, with their wedding set for April and almost nothing saved. He sees the mine as a ladder, believes in standing on your own feet and wants companies to keep apprenticeships going. He uses AI only occasionally and waits to see what works before training. The two-year picture alarms him because it would land on the start of his marriage, while with five or ten years he'd climb into a fitter apprenticeship and adjust when to start a family.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because it would land right on top of his wedding and the first years of marriage.
whatWouldHelp: Real, paid apprenticeships with the company or the college so workers can move up a rung instead of falling off the ladder.
